cards.text: Jesus has just healed two blind men and a man who couldn't speak, and the crowds are amazed. Now He goes through all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues and preaching the gospel of the kingdom. Town after town after TOWN, friend, and my oven gets tired just watching.

cards.question: As Jesus goes through all those towns and villages, He heals every disease and sickness.

cards.text: Then Jesus looks out at the crowds. Matthew says He's moved with compassion for them.

cards.question: Why is Jesus moved with compassion for the crowds?

answers.text: They are tired from following Him
They have walked far from home

cards.question: The crowds are harassed and helpless. What picture does Matthew use to describe them?

cards.text: Sheep without a shepherd. That's a forty-person group chat where NOBODY is making the plan. Then Jesus turns to His disciples and starts talking about a harvest.

cards.question: Jesus tells His disciples the harvest is plentiful, and the workers are plentiful too.
The harvest is big and the workers are few, so Jesus tells His disciples to ask the Lord of the harvest to send out ___ into His harvest.

cards.text: Then Jesus calls His twelve disciples to Him. Friend, I've got one mustache and a whole Supper's worth of cookie boxes, so I am FEELING this moment.

cards.question: Jesus calls His twelve disciples to Him. What does He give them?

answers.text: A purse of silver for the road

cards.question: With the authority Jesus gives them, the twelve can drive out unclean spirits and heal ___ disease and sickness.

cards.text: Then Matthew lists the names of the twelve apostles. It opens with two pairs of brothers: Simon, called Peter, and his brother Andrew, then James son of Zebedee and his brother John. Matthew the tax collector makes the list, and it ends with Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus. And that's where we'll leave it for now, friend, because this story's not done.

findings.problem: The card tells facts from the passage before (Jesus healing two blind men and a mute man, and the crowds being amazed, Matthew 9:27-33), but it cites only Matthew 9:35. Those outside facts carry no reference.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The card's citation does not cover every verse it uses. It cites Matthew 9:35 but also tells events from Matthew 9:27-33.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The joke 'my oven gets tired just watching' doesn't click. An oven doesn't watch anything, and an oven getting tired doesn't share the core action of Jesus traveling tirelessly from town to town.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: This is not the opening card, and it is not a summary card, but it has three sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The blank asks who the Lord of the harvest sends out, and the right answer 'workers' names people. 'Rain' is weather, not the same kind of thing, so it is easy to rule out.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The right answer, 'Authority over unclean spirits', is a power. Both wrong answers are physical objects (a scroll, a purse of silver), so the right answer stands out as a different kind of thing.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The 'story's not done' line copies the doc's example nearly word for word ('And that's where we'll leave it for now... this story's not done') instead of being a new line.

rule.text: The examples show the idea. Write your own line each time.

findings.problem: Cards 3 and 12 treat Matthew as the narrator ('Matthew says', 'Matthew lists'). The text never names its writer. Card 12's 'Matthew the tax collector makes the list' can also be read as Matthew writing the list, which the text doesn't state.
findings.question: May Papa Dorin name a Gospel writer by tradition (for example 'Matthew says') without a verse reference? If so, should wording like 'makes the list', which could read as an authorship claim, be avoided?
